clue.text: Card trick involving ace, the same being turned over in advance

indicators.note: a trick involving other things wraps itself around them, so the trick's letters go outside

parts.note: a con is a swindle or trick

indicators.note: something turned over is upside down, so in a down light the word is read from the bottom up

parts.note: idem is Latin for the same, used in references
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

explanation.surface: A conjuror's card trick in which an ace and its twin are flipped face up before the reveal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In advance' fixes the order inside the trick: the turned-over Latin word goes ahead of the ace. 'Card' is not a playing card at all.
explanation.definitionFit: An amusing, eccentric person is called a card in British slang, and a comic entertainer is the same kind of joker.

clue.text: Take furtive look to observe rears

indicators.note: a horse that rears rises up on its hind legs, so in a down light the word climbs from bottom to top

parts.note: to keep a rule or a festival is to observe it

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks a glance to check out the backsides on view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rears' looks like a noun for backsides but is a verb, rising up, and KEEP climbs to PEEK.
explanation.definitionFit: A peek is a quick sly glance, so to peek is to steal a secret glimpse at something.

clue.text: Drunk? Turf out of employment!

indicators.note: the turf sits out around, on the outside of, the word for employment

parts.note: a sod is a piece of turf
use is employment, as in the employment of a tool

explanation.surface: A boss sacks someone for being drunk on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turf out' reads as sack, but the two words separate: turf is a noun and 'out of' places it around the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: Soused is informal for intoxicated, literally soaked in liquor as fish are pickled in brine.

clue.text: Rabid fan of pop star in frenzy

parts.note: pop and pa are both informal words for father

indicators.note: letters thrown into a frenzy are whirled about wildly and settle in a new order

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A crazed devotee of a pop idol, whipped into a frenzy at a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' looks like music beside 'star', but it is a dad.
explanation.definitionFit: A partisan is a fervent, often one-sided supporter of a cause or party, which a fanatical follower is.

clue.text: Clear floor to provide area for entertainment

parts.note: fair weather is clear weather
the ground is the floor beneath us

explanation.surface: Workers clear a floor space to make room for a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground is the open site where a travelling fair sets up rides and stalls for public amusement.

clue.text: That may be bent grass, eg, covering island

indicators.note: something covering another thing wraps around it, so the outer word goes on either side

parts.note: grass is an example of a plant
I is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: Grass growing over an island, flexible enough to bend in the wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Pliant means flexible or supple, describing something that can be bent without breaking.

clue.text: Guy, as we see it, is grasping

parts.note: cove is old British slang for a man or fellow
to us means in our view

explanation.surface: An opinion that some fellow is greedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Covetous means greedily wanting what belongs to others, the same avarice as grasping.

clue.text: Spot-checks English river rising fast

indicators.note: to check something is to hold it in, so the first word holds the next inside it

parts.note: to spot something is to spy it

indicators.note: in a down light, rising means the word is read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: the Dee flows through Chester in England

explanation.surface: Spot-checks on an English river carried out quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot-checks' reads as one hyphenated noun, but it splits into a verb and a container indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedy is a synonym of fast, meaning moving or done quickly.

clue.text: The French on a horse with a kind of crop

indicators.note: in an across light, one piece sitting on another comes after it, so the French article goes second

parts.note: an Arab is a breed of horse
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A French rider on horseback carrying a riding crop.
explanation.walkthrough: The crop is not a riding whip but a harvest from the fields.
explanation.definitionFit: Arable land is ploughed and used for growing cereals, so it bears that sort of harvest.

clue.text: Have nerve and a bit of bottle

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the narrow part at the top of a bottle

explanation.surface: Have the courage, and a touch of bravery too.
explanation.walkthrough: Bottle is British slang for courage, so the surface reads as nerve and pluck; the bottle is in fact a glass one.
explanation.definitionFit: Neck means impudent boldness in British slang, and it is also the slender upper part of a bottle.

clue.text: Very loud and disturbing, endless noise and natter

indicators.note: disturbing letters knocks them out of place so they settle in a fresh order
without an end means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written, losing its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A complaint about relentless noise and chatter that is loud and unsettling.
explanation.definitionFit: Stentorian describes a powerful booming voice, after Stentor, the herald in Homer's Iliad.

clue.text: It takes pounds to keep one in drink, for example

indicators.note: money that keeps something holds onto it, so the other letter is held within

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pound and quid is slang for pounds
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Staying in drink costs a lot of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pounds' supplies two pound symbols, L and QUID, with I kept between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink is an example of a fluid substance that flows, so it falls under that broader category.

clue.text: Honest reputation succeeds in court

parts.note: someone up before the magistrate is in court
standing is status or reputation

explanation.surface: An honest person's good name wins the day at a trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Succeeds' looks like winning but means comes after, fixing the order of the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstanding citizen is respectable and principled, someone of integrity.

clue.text: Regard "key" (small isle) and "island" as distinct

parts.note: D is a musical key
Is is the short form of island, hence small
Crete is a Greek island

explanation.surface: A geographer insists a key, being a small isle, is a different thing from an island.
explanation.walkthrough: A key is also a low island, so the brackets look like a gloss; in fact key is the note D and 'small isle' is the shortened IS.
explanation.definitionFit: Discrete means separate and individually distinct, not to be confused with discreet.

clue.text: Eats for a stag party?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: snacks or food, informally

definitions.note: cryptic: read as NO SHE'S, no women
definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: no women allowed

explanation.surface: Food laid on for a groom's night out.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it as NO SHES: a stag party is a men-only night out before a wedding, with no women present. The question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Noshes is informal for food or meals, Yiddish in origin, and eats is slang for food.

clue.text: Living with death — machinegun nests in the interior

indicators.note: something that nests in the interior settles down inside, so one word sits within the other

parts.note: exit is a euphemism for death, a departure from life
the Sten was a British submachine gun

explanation.surface: A grim scene of life and death, with gun emplacements hidden inland.
explanation.definitionFit: Existent means in existence, alive and present now, as opposed to extinct.

clue.text: Quite an expression of revulsion following one's volte-face

indicators.note: one thing following another comes after it, so the disgusted noise is placed second
a volte-face is an about-turn, so the word faces the other way

parts.note: taken as written, then turned round
ugh is the noise of disgust

explanation.surface: Someone groans in disgust after a sudden change of mind.
explanation.definitionFit: Enough works as an adverb meaning fairly or sufficiently, as in quite good versus good enough.

clue.text: Do without a man

parts.note: surface reading: manage alone, with no husband or partner
setter's reading: a do is a party, here one where only women attend before a wedding

explanation.walkthrough: 'Do without' reads as a verb phrase, to cope without; in fact 'do' is a noun, a social gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: This British celebration for a bride-to-be and her female friends excludes men, the counterpart of a stag night.

clue.text: This proverb matches putting off with one stealing time

indicators.note: when somebody steals a thing it is taken away, so that letter disappears

parts.note: to stay an execution is to put it off
T is the abbreviation for time; this is the letter stolen

explanation.surface: A proverb comparing procrastination to a thief stealing time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'procrastination is the thief of time'; take T out of STAYING.
explanation.definitionFit: A saying is a short familiar maxim or adage, the same thing as a proverb.

clue.text: Long a head to a Greek department — reportedly a pain in the backside

indicators.note: reported speech is heard rather than read, so the answer is how the words are spoken

parts.note: to long for something is to sigh for it
Attica is the Greek region around Athens

explanation.surface: Someone yearns to head a Greek university department, which turns out to be a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'a head to' as 'ahead of': the sigh comes before Attica. 'A pain in the backside' is literal here.
explanation.definitionFit: Sciatica is nerve pain running from the lower back through the buttock and down the leg.

clue.text: Ingroup get on well together, by the sound of it

indicators.note: the words point to what is heard, so the answer is spelt differently from the word spoken

parts.note: people who click get along instantly

explanation.surface: Members of an exclusive set seem to get along famously.
explanation.definitionFit: A clique is a small exclusive circle of people who keep others out, an insiders' group.

clue.text: Point put about English and, fittingly, by academic

indicators.note: put about means placed around, so the outer word encloses the rest

parts.note: PT is the abbreviation for point

indicators.note: fitted into place suggests the letters are arranged afresh to fit

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A scholar makes a point about English grammar, as you'd expect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fittingly' also comments on the whole: a point about English is just what a stickler would make.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedant is a scholarly type obsessed with minor rules and book learning, a dry academic in the pejorative sense.

clue.text: Yard under pressure, taking long time to uncover plant

indicators.note: the outer pair take in, or hold, the next item between them

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure
an aeon is an immensely long period
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: A garden under pressure takes ages before a plant appears.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light 'under' puts Y below P; AEON then goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The paeony, more often spelt peony, is a garden flower with large showy blooms.

clue.text: Collision involving Jumbo and Harrier, say

definitions.text: Collision involving Jumbo and Harrier, say

parts.note: surface reading: a jumbo jet hitting a Harrier jump jet
setter's reading: a harrier is a hawk, so the jet meets a living flier

explanation.walkthrough: Both names suggest aircraft; 'say' signals that the Harrier is an example of a feathered creature instead.
explanation.definitionFit: This aviation term describes an aircraft hitting a flying animal, a real hazard at take-off and landing.

clue.text: Crackjaw
Beef or fish?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to complain or grumble

explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks a menu question, meat or fish; beef is the verb for grumbling.
explanation.definitionFit: To carp is to complain or nag persistently, and a carp is also a common pond species.

clue.text: Go home and go to bed!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to turn off the road into one's own drive
second meaning: to retire for the night

explanation.surface: A parent's instruction at the end of the evening.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn in means to retire for the night, and also to swing off the road into a gateway or drive.

clue.text: Father and teenager at odds

indicators.note: things at odds are in disagreement and out of line, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: A dad and his adolescent child are not getting on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Father' looks like a noun paired with teenager, but here it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To father is to beget or produce offspring, so it means to bring into being.
